opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most exciting directions, and also one of the hardest. Let me split it into the possibility side and the challenge side.

On the possibility side, every company is a unique environment. It has its own codebase, its own documents, its own workflows, its own unwritten rules about how things get done. Today's general models are strong, but they arrive at a company knowing nothing about it. A human new hire is the same, but a human improves. After three months they know who to ask, which systems are fragile, and what the boss actually means when they say "make it simple." If an agent could accumulate that kind of experience by working inside the company, by doing tasks, getting feedback, and remembering what worked, its value would compound over time instead of staying flat. That's a very different product from a chatbot you query. It's closer to a colleague who keeps getting better.

The challenges, I'd say, are mainly three.

The first is the learning mechanism itself. Today most "learning" in deployed agents is really just stuffing things into context or a retrieval store. That's memory, not learning. Real autonomous learning means the agent can generalize from experience, revise its own beliefs, and not just pile up notes. Doing that reliably, through continual fine-tuning or through better ways of organizing memory, without catastrophic forgetting or drift, is still an open research problem.

The second is the feedback signal. In research we love environments with clear rewards, like math answers or passing unit tests. In a company most tasks don't have a clean verifier. Was this report good? Was this decision right? Feedback is sparse, delayed, noisy, and often political. An agent that learns from bad signals will learn the wrong lessons very efficiently. So designing how the agent gets evaluated inside an organization may matter more than the model architecture.

The third is trust and control. If the agent's behavior keeps changing as it learns, how do you audit it? How do you make sure it doesn't pick up a shortcut that looks productive but violates a policy, or leak information across teams? Companies need to be able to inspect what it learned, roll it back, and set boundaries. Without that, no serious enterprise will let it run autonomously.

So my view is that the base model capability is getting close to good enough. The bottleneck is shifting to the system around the model: memory, feedback loops, evaluation, and governance. Whoever solves that well, the "onboarding and growth" of an agent inside a company, will unlock a lot of value. I don't think it's a one-year problem, but I do think it's the right problem to work on.

r001.rationale: The response compares an agent learning inside a company to a human new hire gaining experience, but it does not discuss transferring learned state or memories between people.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning, feedback, trust, and control, but does not identify merging two learned agents as a systems problem.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually the core question for the next phase of AI, and I'd separate it into two layers.

The first layer is what we have today: a model that is trained once, frozen, and then deployed. It's very capable, but it doesn't change after it leaves the lab. When you put it inside a company, it knows what the internet knows, but it doesn't know your customers, your codebase, your internal processes, the particular way your team makes decisions. We paper over that with retrieval, with long context, with prompts. These work, but they're essentially ways of carrying memory around on the outside of a system that can't itself remember.

The second layer, which I think is the really interesting one, is an agent that actually learns from its own experience inside a specific environment. Not just reads documents, but acts, gets feedback, and updates. A customer service agent that handles ten thousand tickets and genuinely becomes better at that company's tickets, in a way a new one wouldn't be. A coding agent that has lived in your repo for six months and has internalized the conventions nobody ever wrote down.

The possibility there is enormous, because that's where most of the value in an organization actually sits. The tacit knowledge, the stuff that only exists in people's heads. If an agent can accumulate that, you get something closer to an experienced employee than a tool.

But the challenges are real, and I'd be honest that they're not solved.

The first is technical. Continual learning is still unsolved. Every time you update a model on new experience, you risk forgetting, you risk drifting, you risk it getting worse on everything except the narrow thing it just saw. Reinforcement learning in the real world is also very different from RL in a simulator. The feedback is sparse, delayed, noisy, and often wrong. A customer who says "thanks" isn't necessarily satisfied. If the agent learns from that, it learns the wrong lesson.

The second challenge is that a company environment is not static and not well-defined. In a game, the reward is clear. In a company, what counts as "good" is contested, changes quarterly, and depends on who you ask. An agent that optimizes very hard for a badly specified objective will find the gaps. That's not a hypothetical, that's what RL does by definition.

The third is trust and verification. If the agent is changing every day, then what you tested last week isn't what's running today. How do you audit it? How do you roll back? Most companies barely have the infrastructure to evaluate a frozen model properly, let alone one that keeps moving.

And then there's a data question that people underestimate. For this to work, the agent needs to actually be embedded in the workflow, seeing real actions and real outcomes. A lot of companies simply don't have that data in any usable form. Their processes live in email threads and meetings. So before you can even talk about an agent that learns, you often need to rebuild how work is recorded.

So where does that leave me? I'm optimistic on a longer horizon, cautious on the short one. I think the near-term version isn't a fully autonomous learner. It's something in between: an agent with a strong, mostly frozen base, plus a well-designed memory layer, plus a much tighter loop where human feedback is collected deliberately and used to update it in controlled, reviewable steps. Less "it learns on its own," more "it learns with a human in the loop who can see what changed."

The truly autonomous version, where the agent is just living and improving inside your company the way a person would, I think that comes. But it comes after we figure out continual learning as a basic research problem, and after companies rebuild their systems around the idea that an AI is a participant rather than a tool. Both of those are multi-year projects.

r001.rationale: The response compares a learning agent to an experienced employee, but does not discuss transferring an agent’s learned state or memories between agents.

r002.rationale: The response discusses challenges of continual learning, evaluation, and trust, but does not identify merging two learned agents as a systems problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest possibility is an agent that gradually learns how a particular company works—not just its documents, but its processes, priorities, and the reasons behind decisions. That could make it much more useful than a general-purpose assistant. It might notice recurring problems, help people find the right information, and eventually take responsibility for some routine workflows.

But we have to be careful about what we mean by learning. A company generates a lot of activity, and not all of it is worth learning from. People make mistakes, different teams have conflicting goals, and a successful outcome doesn’t necessarily mean the process was good. The agent needs reliable feedback and a way to distinguish an individual preference from a company-wide rule.

There’s also a permissions problem. Learning across departments can be valuable, but it shouldn’t mean that information becomes accessible to everyone. And as the agent changes its behavior, you need to be able to understand those changes, evaluate them, and reverse them if necessary.

So I would start with a narrow workflow where success is measurable and mistakes are recoverable. Let the agent suggest actions, learn from corrections, and earn greater autonomy through demonstrated reliability. The exciting part is that its usefulness could compound over time. The challenge is making sure its reliability compounds along with it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses an agent learning company processes, but it does not compare transferring its learned state to transferring one person’s memories to another.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss merging two learned agents or identify that as a systems problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest possibility is that an agent can gradually learn how a particular company works. A general model may know a lot, but it doesn’t automatically understand your customers, your internal processes, or why your team makes certain decisions. If an agent can learn from that context and from feedback, it could become much more useful over time.

For example, you might start with an agent helping customer support. Initially, it retrieves information and drafts responses for people to review. As it receives corrections, it can learn which information matters, when to ask a follow-up question, and when an issue needs to go to a human. That creates a path from assistance toward greater autonomy.

The challenge is deciding what it should learn and how you know that learning is actually improving its behavior. A successful outcome isn’t always evidence of a good decision, and one employee’s preference may not represent company policy. You also need to control access to sensitive information and prevent mistakes from becoming habits.

So I would start with a narrow task, clear feedback, and limited permissions. Let the agent demonstrate that it is reliable before expanding what it can do. The opportunity is substantial, but the learning process needs to be observable, testable, and reversible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses an agent learning company context and feedback, but does not compare transferring its learned state to transferring one person’s memories to another.

r002.rationale: The response raises challenges around learning, feedback, and permissions, but does not identify merging two learned agents as a difficult systems problem.
